h1: How Much Meat Per Person for Your BBQ
description: Plan your BBQ portions: 400-600g of meat per adult, 250g per child. Free calculator with adjustments for appetite, sides, and meat type.
intro:
Planning a **BBQ** or grill-out and not sure how much meat to buy? This calculator removes the guesswork. Standard catering portions are **400 to 600 grams of raw meat per adult** (roughly **0.9 to 1.3 pounds**) and **200 to 250 grams per child** under 12 (about **0.5 pound**). The exact figure depends on three factors: the **appetite level** of your guests, the **type of meat** you're serving, and what **side dishes** are on the table.

The range is wide for a reason. If you're hosting a backyard cookout where burgers and hot dogs are just one part of a full spread — chips, salads, baked beans, corn, bread, dessert — you can plan toward the lower end, around **400 g per adult**. If grilled meat is the headline (think Texas-style brisket, Argentine asado, Korean galbi, or a wing-night) and sides are an afterthought, push toward **600 g or even 700 g per adult**. Athletic guests, teenage boys and dedicated meat-eaters often go through the higher end without trouble.

Meat type also matters. **Beef and pork** typically need around 500 g per adult because of bone, fat trim and shrinkage during cooking — a 500 g raw steak yields roughly **350–400 g cooked**. **Chicken pieces** with bone-in need around 400–500 g per person (about 2 thighs or 1 breast + 1 drumstick). **Sausages and hot dogs** usually go at 2–3 per adult, equivalent to ~300–400 g. **Brisket and pulled pork** lose around 30–40 % during slow smoking, so plan **550–650 g raw** per adult to end up with ~350 g of finished product on the plate.

A practical rule of thumb: **buy 10 % extra** to cover seconds, leftovers and unexpected guests. Grilled meat reheats well and makes excellent next-day sandwiches, tacos or salads, so erring on the side of "a bit too much" is far better than running out mid-party. The calculator below gives you a total weight estimate based on your headcount; combine it with the meat-type adjustments in this guide for a precise grocery list.
keyTakeaway: **BBQ Meat Portions Calculator**: Standard formula for grilling success. Estimate 400-600g per adult and 250g per child based on appetite and meat type.

Catering professional pricing a wedding reception of 120 guests at $18/person food cost: 120 × 500 g = 60 kg raw meat budget, ~$2,160 in meat alone before sides.
Tailgate party for 8 hungry football fans with burgers + brats: 8 × 600 g = 4.8 kg total — roughly 12 quarter-pound burger patties plus 16 bratwursts (2 each).
Family Sunday cookout for 6 adults + 3 kids with hearty sides (potato salad, coleslaw, corn): drop to 400 g per adult = 2.4 kg + 750 g for kids = 3.15 kg meat total.
Restaurant prepping a family-style grilled platter for tables of 4: 4 × 500 g = 2 kg per platter (mix of ribeye, sausage, chicken thighs) lets you charge $80–120 per table.

Asian-style Korean BBQ for 6 adults with multiple meat types (galbi, bulgogi, pork belly) where small portions of each total ~500 g per person = 3 kg shopping list.

explanation:
## Meat Portions for Grilling

Grilled meat portions vary by appetite, meat type, and what else you're serving. Standard portions are based on decades of catering practices:
- **Adults**: 400-600g per person (hungry eaters: 600g+)
- **Children**: 200-250g per person
- **Side dishes**: portions can go lower if you have hearty sides

## How the Calculator Works

Input the number of adults and children, and get an instant estimate of total meat needed. The calculator uses standard ratios validated across international catering guidelines. Results account for typical appetites but can be adjusted up for very hungry crowds.

## Practical Tips

- Buy slightly extra (5–10%) for waste and second helpings
- Adjust upward if serving mainly meat with few sides
- Factor in meat type: beef requires more than chicken
- Consider appetite levels of your guests

## Final Notes

This is a practical guide based on standard portions. For professional catering, consult with a chef. All values are updated for 2026 and reflect current best practices.

faq.q: How much meat should I buy per person for a BBQ?
faq.a: For a standard backyard BBQ with normal sides, plan on **400–600 g of raw meat per adult** (about 1 to 1.3 lb) and **200–250 g per child** under 12. Adjust upward to 600–700 g per adult if meat is the headline dish with few sides, or if you're hosting athletes, teens or notably hungry guests. Adjust downward to 350–400 g if you're serving lots of hearty sides like potato salad, baked beans, mac and cheese, corn on the cob, garlic bread and dessert. Always buy 10 % extra to cover seconds and unexpected guests.

faq.q: Does the type of meat change how much to buy?
faq.a: Yes, significantly. **Bone-in cuts** (ribs, wings, drumsticks) need about 25 % more weight than boneless because the bone doesn't get eaten — plan ~600 g per adult for ribs versus ~450 g for boneless steak. **Smoked meats** like brisket and pulled pork shrink 30–40 % during cooking, so you need to scale up raw weight accordingly. **Sausages and hot dogs** are easier to count: 2–3 per adult, 1–2 per child. **Chicken breast** (lean) goes further per gram than fatty cuts because there's less shrinkage.

faq.q: What if I have very hungry guests?
faq.a: Increase to **600–700 g per adult**, or even 750 g for groups of athletic young men, manual laborers, or known big eaters. Sports teams, fraternity events and bachelor parties often demand the higher end. A useful heuristic from professional caterers: if you've ever heard one of the guests describe themselves as "someone who can really eat," plan for 1.5 × the standard portion. Better to have leftovers than to run out of food halfway through the party.

faq.q: Should I adjust portions if serving side dishes?
faq.a: Yes. With **plentiful, hearty sides** — potato salad, coleslaw, baked beans, corn, bread, dessert — most guests will fill up halfway through their plate before reaching for seconds of meat. Drop to **350–450 g per adult**. With **minimal sides** (just a salad and bread) or a meat-centric event like a Texas BBQ or an Argentine asado, stay closer to **550–650 g per adult**. The rule of thumb: the more carbs and starches on the table, the less meat people eat.

faq.q: How much shrinkage happens when grilling meat?
faq.a: Meat loses water and fat during cooking. Typical shrinkage rates: **grilled steak or burgers** lose 15–25 % of raw weight, **smoked brisket** loses 30–40 %, **pulled pork shoulder** loses 35–45 %, **whole roasted chicken** loses 25 %, **bratwurst and sausages** lose only 10–15 %. To plan finished portions, divide your target by (1 − shrinkage rate). Example: to end with 350 g of pulled pork per person, buy 350 ÷ 0.6 = ~585 g raw pork shoulder per guest.

faq.q: How many burgers or sausages per person?
faq.a: Standard sizing: **burgers** at 150 g (1/3 lb) each → 2 burgers per adult, 1 per child. **Quarter-pound burgers** (113 g) → 2–3 per adult, 1–2 per child. **Bratwurst or full-size hot dogs** (~85–100 g each) → 2–3 per adult, 1–2 per child. **Cocktail sausages** → 4–6 per adult. **Chicken wings** → 6–8 per adult, 3–4 per child. **Ribs** → about 4 baby back ribs or 3 spare ribs per adult.

Results are practical estimates based on standard catering ratios used by professional event planners, restaurants and home cooks for decades. Real-world variation is roughly **±10 %** based on factors like meat quality, cooking method (high-heat grilling vs. slow smoking), guest demographics (age, gender, activity level) and side-dish abundance. The calculator's output should be treated as a planning starting point — apply the 10 % buffer rule for safety, especially for first-time hosts or unfamiliar guest groups.

faq.q: How do I avoid running out of food?
faq.a: Three rules from professional caterers: (1) always **buy 10 % extra** beyond the calculator estimate to cover seconds, unexpected guests and miscalculations; (2) **front-load the grill** with sausages and chicken pieces in the first hour so early arrivals don't pick over the steaks meant for everyone; (3) keep one or two **backup options** ready — a tray of frozen burger patties, a packet of hot dogs or a pre-cooked rotisserie chicken — that you can deploy if the headline meat runs short. Leftovers reheat well for next-day sandwiches and tacos, so erring on the side of excess is the safe play.

faq.q: Can I calculate portions for just adults or just children?
faq.a: Yes. Enter 0 for the group size you don't have and the calculator will adjust accordingly. If you're hosting only children (a kids' birthday party, for example) plan on 200–250 g per child for ages 6–12 and 150–200 g per child under 6. If your group is all adults, use 400–600 g per adult as the baseline and adjust for appetite and side dishes as described above.

faq.q: What's the best meat for a beginner BBQ host?
faq.a: **Chicken thighs** and **bratwurst sausages** are the most forgiving for new grillers — they have enough fat that they stay juicy even if you slightly overcook them, and they don't require precise temperature management like steak does. **Hot dogs** are essentially foolproof. Avoid **lean cuts** like chicken breast, sirloin steak or pork tenderloin on your first try because they dry out quickly. Avoid **brisket and pulled pork** for beginners — they require 8–14 hours of patient smoking and specialized equipment.

faq.q: How should I store leftover grilled meat?
faq.a: Refrigerate leftovers in shallow airtight containers **within 2 hours** of cooking (1 hour if outdoor temperature is above 32 °C / 90 °F). Grilled meat keeps in the refrigerator for **3 to 4 days**. For longer storage, freeze in portion-sized bags for up to **2 to 3 months**. Reheat gently in a low oven (150 °C / 300 °F) covered with foil to retain moisture, or shred and use in tacos, sandwiches, fried rice, salads or pasta dishes. Pulled pork and brisket actually improve in flavor after a day in the fridge.
